Vandana: Last year you told us you had twelve backup plans. What now?

Sangeeta: Three. I asked which risks are both likely and expensive if they happen: the supplier slipping, our lead developer being out, and the client changing scope. Each has a trigger. If the supplier's parts aren't here by the fifth, we order from the second supplier. If the developer is out two days running, we bring in the contractor.

Vandana: And the rest?

Sangeeta: Gone. And at every milestone we look at the three again. After the first phase the supplier risk was over, so I dropped it and added the test lab being booked out. A short list I actually read beats a long list I don't.

qa.q: What is the trigger for ordering from the second supplier?
qa.a: The trigger is the supplier's parts not being there by the fifth.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta want from the shorter list?
qa.a: Sangeeta wanted a list short enough to read and use, since a long one tends to be ignored.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do if a fourth risk suddenly becomes likely?
qa.a: Sangeeta could add it with a clear trigger and drop or merge the weakest of the others, so that the list stays short.

qa.q: How might a team member see the shorter list?
qa.a: A team member might find it easier to remember and act on, since each trigger is simple and clear.

grounding: Shows a lead keeping three likely and costly contingencies with triggers, and reviewing them at each milestone.

passage:
I'm Deepak, and I work on Farhan's team at the solar installation company. At the start of the rooftop project for the school, his risk list was twenty items long.
Then I watched him cut it. He sat with the list and asked two questions about each item: how likely is this, and how much would it hurt? He kept three. Monsoon rain on install days: if rain is forecast for more than two days, then move the crew to indoor wiring. Panel delivery late: if the truck isn't dispatched by the 10th, then call the second supplier. School exams: if the exam dates are announced, then no drilling during them.
After each stage, he pulled the list out again. After the panels were delivered, he crossed off the delivery line. After exams ended, that one went too.
By the last week, there was only one line left on his whiteboard. He looked relaxed, but I can't be sure.

qa.q: How many risks did Farhan keep from the list of twenty?
What might Farhan looking relaxed in the last week suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt calm and in control, with only one risk left to watch, though Deepak can't be sure.

qa.q: What else could Farhan do at each stage review?
qa.a: He could also ask if any new risk has appeared, so the short list stays accurate and not just smaller.

qa.q: How might the school staff experience Farhan's plan?
qa.a: They get no drilling during exams, so their students can write in peace while the work goes on.

grounding: It shows a project lead keeping three contingencies with clear triggers and reviewing them at each milestone, dropping any that no longer apply.

Week one. Keerthana had just taken over the warehouse move from a colleague who had left a list of nineteen risks. Abhinav, her deputy, sighed. "We'll never plan for all of these."
"We won't," she said. She marked each one for how likely and how costly. Three stood out: trucks not available on moving day, the new racks arriving late, and staff overtime running out. Each got a trigger. If trucks aren't confirmed ten days before, book a second company. If racks aren't shipped by the 5th, rent temporary shelving. If overtime passes forty hours, bring in the weekend temp team.
Week three. The racks were shipped on time. Keerthana crossed that line out in front of Abhinav.
Week five. At the last review, only the overtime rule was left. It triggered once, the temps came in, and the move finished on the planned Saturday.

qa.a: The move finished on the planned Saturday.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel on seeing the list of nineteen risks?
qa.a: Abhinav felt overwhelmed and discouraged, sighing that they would never plan for all of them.

qa.q: Why was crossing out the rack line after it shipped a good step?
qa.a: It kept the list short and focused on what could still go wrong, so attention didn't go to risks that had already passed.

qa.q: How might the staff in the warehouse experience the overtime rule?
qa.a: They get help from the weekend temp team once overtime passes forty hours, so they aren't pushed too far.

grounding: It shows a lead keeping three contingencies with clear triggers and reviewing them at each milestone, dropping ones that no longer apply.
